newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch PTT says gridlock triggered TNT bid.
newsitem.headline: Dutch PTT says gridlock triggered TNT bid.

text.p: Dutch post and telecoms company KPN said it launched this week's 2.7 billion guilder ($1.57 billion) bid for Australia's TNT express mail operation because of fears that Europe states would resist efforts to free up their ageing postal monopolies.

"There will be no (postal) liberalisation in Europe. Things are moving backwards rather than ahead, that's why we made this bid," PTT Post director Ad Scheepbouwer said in an interview late on Thursday.

EU nations have yet to agree a plan for pan-European mail liberalisation although the EU Commission is pushing for action by the start of 2001 on direct mail and cross-border mail. Some nations oppose moving that fast.
PTT Post is one half of KPN -- Koninklijke PTT Nederland (KPN/Dutch PTT) which made its bid for TNT on Wednesday.
The move underlines KPN's aggressive expansion out of the modest Dutch domestic market and could pose a challenge to its giant European rivals -- Deutsche Telekom and Britain's Royal Mail.
They are in danger of being left behind as the Dutch group emerges from state control to steal a march in Europe's fast-growing mail business, alongside FedEx, United Parcel Service (UPS) and DHL.
By adding Australian-based TNT, which is active in Europe, KPN will double its postal activities to 13 billion guilders, half of total sales.
This is exciting growth when compared with the almost stagnant ordinary mail services in Europe.
In Asia, where TNT is one of a few global players of any size, time-sensitive distribution of letters and packages is seen growing at an even faster rate -- at over 20 percent.
Despite the boom market, TNT profits have disappointed in recent years, but KPN said its biggest gains would come from mering TNT and an existing joint venture, GD Express Worldwide.

"Until now TNT was not allowed to deliver cross-border express mail, while GD was limited to international services," Scheepbouwer said. "Soon, a package deposited in Berlin will be sent to either Hamburg or Antwerp by one company."

He said TNT would start contributing to KPN profits in 1997, even after deducting interest paid on a 2.25 billion guilder revolving credit facility. Annual cost saving gains could be 125 million guilders by 1999.
Scheepbouwer promised major benefits from combining TNT's entrepreneurial spirit and PTT Post's own solid structure.
"The premium we're paying on TNT shares will certainly prove worthwhile after we've yielded all the synergies," he said.
PTT has offered $A2.45 a TNT share, a 48 percent premium over the pre-offer market price. "This was in the middle of the range PTT was prepared to pay", Scheepbouwer said.
He said KPN carried out only limited due diligence on TNT, relying mainly on information widely available to the public.

He said the offer had been made for TNT's express mail and logistics operations, adding that KPN could only take a closer look at other, mainly loss-making, activities once it had acquired all the shares.
One business KNP regards as non-core is an Australian freight transport service with annual sales of A$700-800 million.
"That's the kind of company we'll take a close look at. But at a possible sale we won't suffer any nasty surprises (losses) as we've been conservative in our calculations," he said.
Scheepbouwer said talks on a possible bid began earlier this summer but PTT Post waited to make its offer until TNT had disposed of its Ansett passenger airline on October 1.
KPN will still control Ansett's aircraft leasing business, the third largest in the world, which may be sold or run down, Scheepbouwer said.

Market specialists, who have qualified the TNT buy as threatening KNP's relative income stability from postal activities, could be surprised by the performance of TNT's logistics operations, Scheepbouwer said.
For the time being at least, KPN plans to keep TNT's brandname as well as other strong market tags, such as KPN's express service (EMS).
